title: The 12 Skills Worth Installing for SEO Work
description: A working SEO stack for agent-assisted sites — ordered by the stage of the job you'd actually use each one at, not by download count.
targetKeyword: best SEO skills for Claude Code

curator.name: TrustedSkills Editorial
curator.bio: Curated with input from a decade of hands-on agency SEO work across technical audits, content strategy and programmatic builds.

intro:
There are close to 400 skills in this registry that mention SEO somewhere. Almost none of that is useful as a shopping list, because SEO isn't one job — it's six or seven different jobs that happen in a rough order, and a skill that's excellent at the fourth one is useless if you haven't done the first.

So this list isn't "the 12 most installed SEO skills". It's a stack: one or two picks per stage of an actual SEO engagement, in the order you'd reach for them. If you install all twelve you have coverage from first crawl to measurement. If you install the first three you have the 80% that matters on a site nobody has audited yet.

The stages, in order: **diagnose → fix the technical floor → fix the page → structure the data → find the demand → study the competition → earn authority → optimise for AI search → measure**.
criteria:
**How the twelve were chosen.** Each pick had to (1) be present in this registry with a resolvable source repository, (2) do one clearly-defined job rather than being a general marketing assistant, and (3) occupy a distinct stage in the workflow above — no two picks doing the same job.

Where two skills competed for the same slot, the tiebreak was publisher track record and install base, both visible on each card below.

**What changed after testing.** We ran the original twelve on our own site in September 2026. Three got a Not Recommended verdict: `on-page-seo-auditor` and `backlink-analyzer` no longer install under their listed names, and their author has frozen them in favour of renamed skills; `seo-meta` was deleted by its author, and its templates only fit a local trade business. A list called "worth installing" should not include skills we tell you not to install, so we replaced them. Their reviews are still published, so you can read why.

**What we deliberately left off.**

- **Programmatic SEO skills.** There's a well-installed `programmatic-seo` skill in the registry and it is genuinely capable. It's off this list on purpose: pointing an agent at page generation before you've fixed a site's technical floor is the fastest way to manufacture an index-bloat problem. It belongs in a later collection, not a starter twelve.
- **All-in-one marketing suites.** Several broad suites include an SEO module. They're reasonable buys, but they make it hard to tell which part of the toolchain you're actually using.
- **Niche vertical skills.** App-store optimisation and research-lab-specific SEO skills are both in the registry and both fine at their job — just not part of a general web SEO stack.
- **Anything we couldn't trace to a source.** If we couldn't open the repository, it didn't make the list.
evidenceNote:
**Nine of the twelve were hands-on tested by us, once each, on the same site (trustedskills.dev) in September 2026.** Each of those cards links to its full review, and the verdict and score on the card come from that run. One run on one site is one data point, not a benchmark.

**The other three are replacement picks and have not been tested yet**: `agricidaniel-seo-page`, `seo` and `build-links`. We chose them from their source and documentation, publisher and install base, the same basis the whole list started from. They are next in our review queue, and their cards will carry a 🧪 **Reviewed** badge once they have been run.

Three of the tested picks were renamed or moved upstream, so the registry's install command for them no longer works. Those cards carry a warning, and each note below gives the command that worked for us.

entries.note: The most-installed SEO skill in the registry, and it earned its place. Working from nothing but page fetches and a web search, it found two separate indexing bugs on our site and put them at the top of its list, where they belonged. It is current (INP, not FID) and says where its own checks can fail. It can't do Core Web Vitals, backlinks or a full-site crawl on its own, which is what the rest of this list is for.

Where the previous pick gives you a strategic read, this one puts a real crawler behind your agent: 260-plus rules across SEO, performance, security and accessibility. On our site it found things the page-fetch skills missed, such as a broken docs link and missing security headers. It also missed the canonical error that four simpler skills caught, and one of the three findings we checked was a false positive. Run it alongside stage 1, not instead of it.

Crawl, indexing, speed and mobile checks with clear P0/P1/P2 severities. In our run it found the most damaging defect of all twelve: a site-wide canonical tag pointing every page at the homepage. It uses INP, not FID, and it won't invent metrics it can't measure. The skill has moved repositories, so the listed command fails; `npx skills add aaron-he-zhu/aaron-marketing-skills -s technical-seo-checker` worked for us. Installed alone, its helper scripts are missing.

The most disciplined skill we tested. It measures before it advises, keeps lab and field numbers apart, uses INP rather than the retired FID, and won't call a metric failing without evidence. On our homepage it traced LCP, layout shift and main-thread cost to specific elements and scripts. It points to measurement guides in a sibling `performance` skill from the same publisher, Addy Osmani, so install both.

Once the site-wide floor is solid, the work becomes page by page. This is the single-page module of the claude-seo suite: title, meta, headings, internal links, content quality, schema and images for one URL. We have run the full claude-seo audit, and its review is published, but we have not yet tested this module installed on its own. Its checks call the suite's helper scripts, so expect some to be skipped if you install only this skill. Not yet tested by us.

entries.role: Stage 3 — Fix the page (titles, meta and headings)
entries.note: Titles and meta descriptions are still some of the highest-leverage lines on a page. This skill from Addy Osmani's `web-quality-skills` covers them, plus headings, images and internal links, and it starts from Lighthouse evidence rather than rules of thumb. Its guidance treats the 50–60 character title length as a rough proxy, not a hard limit, and it tells the agent not to promise ranking changes. Same publisher as the stage 2 performance pick. Not yet tested by us.

It only marked up what the page actually shows, which is the most important thing a schema generator can do. The JSON-LD it wrote was valid, it caught a redirect bug in our existing markup, and it declined to add ratings or prices we don't have. It was renamed upstream: install it with `npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills --skill schema`. It lists FAQPage and HowTo with no warning about Google's rich-result limits on them, so check before you ship those.

A sound keyword-research method in one file: intent, tiers, clusters, and a cannibalisation check before you build anything. It installed first time and ran cleanly. But its output is built around search volume and difficulty, and it doesn't tell you where to get them. With no data source connected you get a well-structured list with the numbers missing. Worth it if you already have a volume source behind an MCP server.

A tidy playbook for featured snippets, People Also Ask and rich results. The page-level advice it gave us was concrete. But its first step assumes you can see a live Google results page, and it has no fallback. Without a SERP data source you get good formatting advice and no evidence about which features are really there. This is still the step most people skip, so it keeps its slot. Connect a SERP source before you rely on it.

Our test of the previous pick taught us that backlink analysis without a paid link database has nothing to analyse. This skill does the other half of the job: it diagnoses which kind of authority a site is short of, then designs a campaign around linkable assets, prospects and outreach. That work doesn't need a link database to start. Calibrate expectations: it plans link acquisition, it doesn't do it. From `calm-north/seojuice-skills`, the same publisher as stage 5. Not yet tested by us.

The most useful AI search skill we tested. It separates Google's stated position (write for people, no special AI markup) from what ChatGPT, Perplexity and agents actually reward. Its audit found real problems on our site, and the free scanner it names worked as written. Two cautions: several headline statistics in the skill have no source, and no skill can tell you whether you are being cited without access to the AI platforms themselves.

Last on the list and not optional: without measurement the other stages are opinion. On our site it produced a practical GA4 event plan, and found that our two most important user actions were not tracked at all. It was renamed upstream: install it with `npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills --skill analytics`. It has no workflow for auditing a site whose dashboards you can't open, so pair it with Search Console access.
